title: Smooth time-dependent control of dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates
authors: Chris Whitty, Aitor Alaña, Michele Modugno, Xi Chen, Géza Tóth, Andreas Ruschhaupt, Eugene Ya. Sherman
abstract: We consider protocols for control of dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates where the critical role is played by the long-range anisotropic interatomic magnetic dipole-dipole interaction. The phase diagram of such a condensate has been explored theoretically and experimentally with certain values of the interatomic scattering length corresponding to superfluid and supersolid phases, where supersolidity appears as a modulation in the ground state density. Preparation of this modulated ground state is challenging, since excitations appear as a result of a finite-time evolution required to produce qualitative changes in the wavefunction density. To solve this problem we consider the time-dependent control of a dipolar Bose-Einstein condensate using shortcuts to adiabaticity techniques, concentrating on design of the time-dependent scattering length, a parameter of the system easily tunable by contemporary experiments. The first technique is the variational approach based on the Euler-Lagrange equations for a separable ansatz describing the evolution of the superfluid state. Secondly, we study the transition from superfluid to supersolid using a direct optimization protocol. We discuss the fidelity of the developed protocols in terms of the evolution time.
summary: The paper develops sophisticated time-dependent control protocols using Shortcuts to Adiabaticity techniques to manipulate dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates across their superfluid-to-supersolid phase transition. By employing variational and direct optimization methods, the authors design smooth changes in the scattering length that minimize excitations and maintain high fidelity throughout the process.
main_problem: The primary goal is designing smooth time-dependent control protocols for dipolar Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) to manage the transition between superfluid and supersolid phases while minimizing excitations.
main_result:
Variational approaches combined with direct numerical optimization successfully design control profiles, such as $a^{(
u)}_s(t)$, that achieve high fidelity ($F_{\min} \gtrsim 0.95$) and suppress unwanted probability currents during the phase transition.
method: The study employs Shortcuts to Adiabaticity (STA) techniques, utilizing a variational approach with inverse engineering (VAIE) for superfluid regimes and direct optimization protocols for the challenging superfluid-supersolid transition.
model_or_system: The system is dipolar BECs, modeled by an extended Gross-Pitaevskii equation (eGPE). The Hamiltonian includes kinetic energy, external potential, long-range anisotropic dipole-dipole interaction (DDI), and tunable contact interactions. Control is exerted via the time-dependent s-wave scattering length, $a_s(t)$.
key_observables: Time-dependent target-overlap fidelity ($F_T(t)$) and its minimum value ($F_{\min}$); probability density current ($\mathbf{j}_x(x, t)$); Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).
important_parameters: The critical scattering length $a_c$ that separates the superfluid and supersolid phases; the control time duration ($t_f$).
main_assumptions: The variational ansatz used in the VAIE method is assumed to be separable, which limits its accuracy near the phase transition. Spherical truncation of the dipole interaction was also considered.
figures_summary: Figures compare current density snapshots ($\mathbf{j}_x$) showing flow suppression by optimized schemes versus oscillations from polynomial schemes; fidelity plots show $F_{\min}$ comparisons across various control protocols.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the eGPE model, details the use of STA techniques, applies a variational approach for superfluid evolution, and then uses direct optimization to design robust controls specifically for crossing the superfluid-supersolid phase boundary.
why_interesting: This work represents an advanced application of optimal control theory to highly interacting quantum many-body systems. The ability to precisely guide a system through a quantum phase transition while minimizing excitations is crucial for realizing novel quantum states in cold atom experiments.
